fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that gets me most excited about it is that it turns evaluation from a static thing into a dynamic thing. For most of the history of NLP benchmarks, you have a fixed input and a fixed output, and you check whether the model got it right. But that's just not what deploying an agent in the real world looks like. If you're an airline customer service agent, the customer doesn't hand you a fully specified request on turn one. They tell you part of it, they forget details, they change their mind halfway through, sometimes they ask for something the policy doesn't allow. The agent has to elicit information, clarify, push back politely, and still get the task done.

So what we did in Tau Bench is have a language model play the user. We give it a scenario, something like, you're this person, you want to change your flight, but you only remember your confirmation number if the agent asks, and you're going to be a little annoyed about the fees. And then the agent model has to actually have that conversation. What I find exciting is that it gives you a much more faithful picture of where agents actually break. A lot of the failures we see aren't about the model not knowing how to call a tool. They're about the model not asking the right question, or taking an action before it has enough information, or getting talked into violating a policy because the simulated user was persistent.

The other piece that I think is underrated is that the simulation lets you measure reliability, not just capability. Because the user is stochastic, you can run the same task many times and ask, does the agent succeed every time, or does it succeed one time out of four? That's where our pass^k metric comes from. And honestly, the numbers there were kind of sobering. Models that look decent on a single run fall off a cliff when you ask them to be consistent. For anything you'd actually deploy, consistency is the whole game.

Now, I'll be the first to say the user simulator is also the weakest link. If the simulated user is too cooperative, you're overestimating the agent. If it's incoherent, you're punishing the agent for something that's not its fault. So a lot of the ongoing work is about making those simulated users more faithful, more diverse, and harder to game. But I think the basic move, putting a simulated human in the loop so that the benchmark is interactive, is one that's going to stick around. It's really the only way to evaluate the stuff that makes agents hard.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the user simulation is the part I'm proudest of, because it's what makes the benchmark feel like the real world rather than a puzzle.

Most agent benchmarks before Tau Bench gave the agent a fully specified task up front: here's the instruction, go call some tools, and we check the output. Real deployments don't work that way. When you put an agent in front of customers, say for an airline or a retailer, the person on the other end doesn't hand you a clean spec. They reveal information a bit at a time. They forget their order number. They change their mind halfway through. Sometimes they ask for things the policy doesn't allow. So the agent has to do two things at once: hold a natural conversation to figure out what the person actually wants, and take correct actions through APIs while following a fairly complicated set of domain rules.

So we use a language model to play the user. Each task gives it a hidden goal and a persona, and it talks to the agent the way a person would. What's exciting is that this makes evaluation dynamic. Every run is a slightly different conversation, even for the same task, and that's realistic. It's also what let us measure something I think matters a lot more than people realized at the time, which is reliability. We introduced the pass^k metric: not "can the agent solve this once," but "can it solve the same task correctly k times in a row across different conversations." When you look at it that way, a lot of agents that look decent on a single try fall off a cliff. For a business deploying this to millions of customers, that consistency is everything.

The other nice part is that because the user is simulated but the backend is a real database, we can grade objectively. We don't need a judge model to decide whether the conversation "went well." We compare the final database state against the expected one. Did the reservation actually get changed correctly? Was the refund issued according to policy? That combination, a messy natural-language front end with a crisp, verifiable outcome, is what makes it useful.

And we've kept pushing on it. In later versions we gave the user tools too, so in something like a telecom troubleshooting scenario both the agent and the user can act on the environment, and the agent has to guide the person through steps on their end. That's much closer to how real support works, where the problem gets solved jointly.

It isn't perfect. Simulated users can sometimes behave in ways a real human wouldn't, and we've spent a lot of time making the simulator more faithful. But I think simulating the human in the loop is going to be central to how we evaluate and train agents going forward, because the human is where most of the real-world complexity lives.

fable-5.text:
Yeah, so the user simulation is actually, I think, the most interesting part of Tau Bench, and it's what sets it apart from a lot of the agent benchmarks that came before it. Most benchmarks up to that point were static — you give the agent a fully specified task upfront, it goes off and executes, and you check the final state. But that's not how real interactions work, right? In a real customer service scenario, the user doesn't dump all the information on you at once. They might not remember their order number, they might change their mind halfway through, they might ask for something that's actually against policy.

So what we did was use a language model to simulate the user, with a hidden instruction describing what they actually want. And that creates this dynamic, two-sided interaction where the agent has to elicit information, ask clarifying questions, and sometimes push back — like, "I'm sorry, I can't give you a refund on that item because of the return policy." The agent isn't just calling tools against a database; it's navigating a conversation while following domain rules.

What I find most exciting is two things. First, it lets us measure something much closer to real-world deployment. The agent has to be robust to the messiness of natural dialogue — the user simulator will phrase things differently every time, withhold details, and so on. And second, because the interaction is stochastic, we could define this pass-hat-k metric, where we ask: does the agent succeed not just once, but consistently across multiple trials of the same task? And what we found was pretty striking — even the best models at the time would succeed maybe sixty percent of the time on retail tasks, but if you required them to succeed eight times in a row, that number dropped dramatically. That gap between "can do it once" and "does it reliably" is exactly what matters if you're actually going to deploy these agents, and it's something you simply can't see without a simulated user in the loop.

Of course, the simulation isn't perfect — the simulated user can occasionally behave in weird ways, and that's an open research problem in itself. But I think this general recipe, using LLMs to simulate the human side of the interaction, is going to be essential for evaluating agents at scale going forward.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, the user simulator started as a means to an end and turned into the part I think about most.

The original motivation was pretty mundane. Almost every agent benchmark at the time handed the model a complete, well-specified instruction and then graded the output. But that's not what happens when you deploy something as a customer service agent. The person on the other end doesn't know your refund policy, doesn't have their reservation ID in front of them, and will tell you about the second thing they wanted only after you've already solved the first. So if you want to measure whether an agent can actually do that job, you need something on the other side of the conversation that behaves like a person. And you can't put humans in the loop at the scale you need for an eval.

What surprised us is how much that one change exposes. Once the information lives with the user instead of in the prompt, the agent has to go get it, which means asking good questions, and a lot of models are strikingly bad at that. They'd rather guess and act than ask. The other direction matters too: the agent has to explain the policy back, confirm before it does something irreversible. We saw models that could call the right tool but couldn't tell the user what they'd done.

And then you get these emergent moments where the simulated user pushes back, asks for an exception, applies a little social pressure, and you find out whether the model's rule-following was real or just a default it holds when nobody's objecting. That was never a design goal. It fell out of the setup.

The flip side, which I'd be lying to skip, is that the simulator becomes part of what you're measuring. If it breaks character or volunteers something it shouldn't, you're scoring noise. A lot of the work since has been about making it faithful and diverse enough that the variance you see is the agent's, not the simulator's.

sonnet-5.5.text:
What excites me most is that the user simulation lets us test something static benchmarks can't: an agent holding a real, multi-turn conversation with someone who doesn't hand over everything up front.

In most agent benchmarks, you give the model a fully specified task and it goes off and uses tools. That's not how people behave. A real customer doesn't say, "Here is my order ID, here is the exact item I want to exchange, and here is the policy that applies." They reveal information gradually, they're a bit vague, and they change their minds. Sometimes they ask for something the policy doesn't allow. So in Tau Bench we use a language model to play the user. It gets a scenario with a goal and some private information, and it only shares that as the conversation unfolds. The agent has to ask the right questions, follow the domain rules, call the right tools, and not get talked into doing something it shouldn't.

Because the user is simulated, we can run many different conversations for the same underlying task. That's what makes the reliability question interesting. It's one thing for an agent to succeed once. It's another to succeed every time across many trials of the same scenario, with the user phrasing things differently each time. When we looked at that, even strong models dropped off a lot. A customer-facing agent that works 60% of the time isn't something you can deploy.

Simulated users aren't perfect, and I don't think they replace real people. But they're a scalable, reproducible way to get at the interactive, messy part of the problem. I think that's where a lot of the remaining gap is between agents that look good in demos and agents you'd trust in production.

astra-6.text:
I think the most exciting part is that you can evaluate an interaction, rather than just a single answer. A user comes in with a goal, but they may not give you all the information up front. The agent has to ask questions, understand the responses, and figure out how to move the conversation forward.

With a simulated user, you can explore different ways that interaction might unfold. What happens if the user is unclear? What happens if the agent makes a mistake and needs to recover? Those are really interesting capabilities to test, because being useful isn’t just about knowing the right answer. It’s about being able to work with someone to get something done.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most exciting part is that the user becomes part of the environment. Instead of giving an agent a fixed question and checking its answer, you can look at how an entire interaction unfolds. Does the agent ask for clarification when something is missing? Does it understand the response and adjust what it’s doing? Does it actually help the user accomplish their goal?

That’s a much richer thing to evaluate, because a lot of the difficulty is in that back-and-forth. A request might seem straightforward initially, but you discover the constraints through the conversation.

And simulation gives you the possibility of exploring lots of those interactions repeatedly. Of course, the important question is how well the simulated users capture real user behavior. But that’s what makes it interesting: you’re starting to evaluate the agent’s ability to collaborate with someone over time.
